summary.text: For a set whose pairwise sums involve only \(k\) primes, the proof studies the reduced denominators of \(2a/(a+b)\): a normalized Cauchy-determinant argument bounds each high prime-power denominator ball by \(4k^2\), while a denominator quasi-triangle inequality covers all positive elements by two families of \(k\) such balls, giving \(|A|\le 16+8k^3\) (including a possible zero). Applying this to the prime support of the restricted-sum product yields \(n\le16+8f(n)^3\), so \(f(n)\gg n^{1/3}\) and therefore \(f(n)/\log n\to\infty\).

full_proof.text:
We prove the stated assertion. The main point is a quantitative result: if all pairwise sums from a finite set of natural numbers have their prime factors in a fixed set of k primes, then the set has at most 16+8k^3 elements. We first establish this bound.

Throughout, if q is a rational number, write den(q) for the positive denominator of q in lowest terms. For a prime p, write |.|_p for the usual p-adic norm, normalized by |p|_p=p^{-1}.

1. A normalized Cauchy determinant

For distinct positive rational numbers b_1,...,b_m, consider the m by m matrix

  C=(C_ij),    C_ij = 2b_i/(b_i+b_j).

Its determinant is

  det C = product_{1<=i<j<=m} ((b_i-b_j)/(b_i+b_j))^2.                 (1)

Here is a direct derivation. The diagonal entries are 1. If a positive number a is singled out and the remaining numbers are denoted b_i, the Schur complement of the top-left entry 1 has entries

  2b_i/(b_i+b_j) - (2b_i/(b_i+a))(2a/(a+b_j)).

A direct simplification gives

  2b_i/(b_i+b_j) - (2b_i/(b_i+a))(2a/(a+b_j))
   = ((b_i-a)/(b_i+a)) (2b_i/(b_i+b_j)) ((b_j-a)/(b_j+a)).

Thus the Schur complement is obtained from the smaller normalized Cauchy matrix by multiplying row i and column i by (b_i-a)/(b_i+a). Consequently,

  det C_m = product_i ((b_i-a)/(b_i+a))^2 det C_{m-1}.

Induction on m proves (1).

Since the b_i are positive and distinct, every factor on the right of (1) is positive. Moreover,

  |b_i-b_j| < b_i+b_j,

so each squared factor is at most 1. We therefore have

  0 < det C <= 1.                                                     (2)

Formula (1) also gives a useful p-adic estimate. Suppose that rho>=0 and

  |(b_i-b_j)/(b_i+b_j)|_p <= rho

for every i!=j. There are m(m-1)/2 unordered pairs and every corresponding factor is squared, so

  |det C|_p <= rho^{m(m-1)}.                                         (3)

2. A p-adic denominator-ball estimate

Fix a prime p, a positive integer e, a positive rational anchor a, and distinct positive rationals b_1,...,b_m. Suppose

  p^e divides den(2a/(a+b_i))                                        (4)

for every i. We claim that this forces a strong divisibility property on the normalized Cauchy determinant associated with the b_i.

Put

  t_i=(a+b_i)/(2a).

This is the reciprocal of 2a/(a+b_i). Since that latter rational is in lowest terms and its denominator is divisible by p^e, its numerator is not divisible by p. Hence

  |t_i|_p <= p^{-e}.                                                  (5)

For i!=j, a direct algebraic identity is

  (b_i-b_j)/(b_i+b_j)
   = (t_i-t_j)/(t_i+t_j-1).                                          (6)

Let rho=p^{-e}<1. By the ultrametric inequality and (5),

  |t_i+t_j|_p <= rho < 1.

Therefore |t_i+t_j-1|_p=1: a number of p-adic norm strictly below 1 cannot cancel the unit 1. Also |t_i-t_j|_p<=rho. Equation (6) consequently yields

  |(b_i-b_j)/(b_i+b_j)|_p <= p^{-e}.

Applying (3),

  |det C|_p <= p^{-m(m-1)e}.                                         (7)

Now suppose, in addition, that every entry C_ij has reduced denominator dividing a positive integer Q. Multiplying every entry by Q produces an integral matrix. Thus

  z=Q^m det C

is an integer. By (2),

  0<z<=Q^m.                                                          (8)

Since |Q|_p<=1, (7) gives

  |z|_p<=p^{-m(m-1)e},

which means

  p^{m(m-1)e} divides z.

Combining this with (8),

  p^{m(m-1)e} <= Q^m.

The left side is (p^{(m-1)e})^m. Taking m-th roots in the nonnegative integers gives the denominator-ball estimate

  p^{(m-1)e} <= Q.                                                    (9)

3. High prime-power balls are small

Let k,T,Q be positive integers satisfying

  Q<=T^k.

Fix an anchor a and a prime p. Define the high p-power ball around a to consist of those positive rational vertices b for which

  T < p^{4k e_b},    where e_b=v_p(den(2a/(a+b))).                   (10)

Suppose that m distinct vertices lie in this ball and that all normalized Cauchy denominators between those vertices divide Q. Choose

  e=min_b e_b.

Condition (10) implies e>=1 and

  T<p^{4ke}.                                                         (11)

Every vertex in the ball satisfies p^e | den(2a/(a+b)), so (9) gives

  p^{(m-1)e}<=Q<=T^k.                                                (12)

We claim that

  m<=4k^2.                                                           (13)

Indeed, if m>4k^2, then m-1>=4k^2. Raising (11) to the k-th power and using (12) would give

  T^k < p^{4k^2e} <= p^{(m-1)e} <= Q <= T^k,

an impossibility. This proves (13).

4. A quasi-triangle inequality for normalized denominators

For positive rationals a,b,c, set

  d(a,b)=den(2a/(a+b)).

We need the inequality

  d(a,b) < 2 d(a,c)d(b,c).                                          (14)

To prove it, first observe the algebraic identity

  2a/(a+b)
   = [r(2-s)]/[r+s-rs],

where

  r=2a/(a+c),    s=2b/(b+c).

Both r and s lie strictly between 0 and 2. Write r=R/x and s=S/y in lowest terms, where x=den(r), y=den(s). The displayed rational expression can be represented with integer denominator

  L=Ry+Sx-RS.

Indeed, r+s-rs=L/(xy), while the corresponding numerator is R(2y-S). Moreover,

  0<r+s-rs<2.

The positivity follows, for example, by writing

  2(r+s-rs)=r(2-s)+s(2-r),

whose two summands are positive. The upper bound follows similarly from

  2-(r+s-rs)=[(2-r)(2-s)+rs]/2>0.

Thus

  0<L<2xy.

The reduced denominator of r(2-s)/(r+s-rs) divides L, and hence is at most L. This proves (14).

We will combine (14) with the following elementary real inequality. If T>=4, x,y>0, and

  T<2xy,

then

  T<x^4 or T<y^4.                                                    (15)

For if x^4<=T and y^4<=T, then

  x^2y^2 <= (x^4+y^4)/2 <= T,

so xy<=sqrt(T). Since T>=4, 2sqrt(T)<=T, contradicting T<2xy.

5. A cubic bound from normalized denominator support

Let b_1,...,b_n be distinct positive rationals. Suppose that every number

  d(i,j)=den(2b_i/(b_i+b_j))

has all of its prime factors in a fixed finite set S of primes. Put k=|S|. We prove

  n<=15+8k^3.                                                        (16)

Let

  T=max_{i,j} d(i,j).

First consider the case T>=4. We construct a common denominator Q for all the d(i,j) as follows. For each p in S, let E_p be the maximum of v_p(d(i,j)) over all ordered pairs (i,j), and set

  Q=product_{p in S} p^{E_p}.

Every d(i,j) divides Q, because its prime support is contained in S and each of its p-adic exponents is at most E_p. Furthermore,

  Q<=T^k.                                                           (17)

Indeed, for each p, some d(i,j) attains exponent E_p; hence p^{E_p} divides that positive integer d(i,j), so p^{E_p}<=d(i,j)<=T. Multiplying these k inequalities proves (17).

Choose u,v for which d(u,v)=T. We cover all vertices using high prime-power balls around u and v.

Fix an arbitrary i. By (14),

  T=d(u,v)<2d(u,i)d(v,i).

By (15), either

  T<d(u,i)^4

or

  T<d(v,i)^4.                                                       (18)

Suppose the first alternative holds; the second is identical with v in place of u. Since the prime support of d(u,i) is contained in S,

  d(u,i)=product_{p in S} p^{v_p(d(u,i))}.

At least one p in S must satisfy

  T<p^{4k v_p(d(u,i))}.                                             (19)

Otherwise, multiplying the inequalities p^{4k v_p(d(u,i))}<=T over p in S would give

  d(u,i)^{4k}<=T^k.

But T<d(u,i)^4, raised to the k-th power, gives the strict reverse inequality T^k<d(u,i)^{4k}. Thus (19) holds.

Consequently every vertex i belongs to a high p-power ball, for some p in S, around at least one of the two anchors u and v. For each fixed anchor and fixed prime, Section 3 shows that this ball has at most 4k^2 vertices: its internal normalized denominators all divide Q, and (17) supplies the required budget Q<=T^k. There are k possible primes and two anchors. Hence

  n<=2k(4k^2)=8k^3                                                    (20)

when T>=4. Notice also that in this case S cannot be empty, since T>=4 has a prime divisor.

It remains to treat T<=3. Fix any vertex c and consider

  q_i=2b_i/(b_i+b_c).

Each q_i lies strictly between 0 and 2, and den(q_i)<=3. If q_i=N_i/D_i in lowest terms, positivity gives N_i>=1, while q_i<2 and D_i<=3 give N_i<2D_i<=6, so N_i<=5. Thus the reduced numerator-denominator pair (N_i,D_i) lies among the 15 pairs

  1<=N_i<=5,    1<=D_i<=3.

The map b -> 2b/(b+b_c) is injective for positive b: equality of the two fractions and cancellation of the positive b_c immediately gives equality of the b's. Therefore the q_i are distinct and n<=15. Together with (20), this proves (16) in all cases.

6. From normalized denominators to pairwise sums

Let a_1,...,a_n be distinct positive integers, and suppose every off-diagonal sum a_i+a_j has all prime factors in S. Regard the a_i as positive rationals. For i=j,

  2a_i/(a_i+a_i)=1,

whose denominator has no prime factors. For i!=j, the reduced denominator of

  2a_i/(a_i+a_j)

divides a_i+a_j: before reduction, the displayed fraction has denominator a_i+a_j, and reduction can only decrease it by a divisor. Hence every prime factor of the reduced denominator belongs to S. Applying (16) gives

  n<=15+8|S|^3                                                       (21)

for sets of positive integers.

A set A of natural numbers can contain zero, but at most once. Applying (21) to A\{0} gives

  |A|<=16+8|S|^3,                                                    (22)

provided every sum of two distinct elements of A has prime support in S.

7. Apply the bound to the restricted-sum product

For a finite set A of natural numbers define

  P(A)=product_{(a,b) in A^2, a!=b} (a+b).

This is exactly the product in the problem; ordered pairs are used, but that does not affect its set of prime divisors. Every factor in this product is positive. Indeed, two distinct natural numbers cannot both be zero, so a+b>0 whenever a!=b. Thus P(A)>0, including the empty-product cases.

Let S be the set of distinct prime divisors of P(A), and write

  k=|S|.

For any distinct a,b in A, the number a+b is one of the factors of P(A), so a+b divides P(A). Every prime divisor of a+b therefore belongs to S. Applying (22),

  |A|<=16+8k^3
      =16+8(number of distinct prime divisors of P(A))^3.             (23)

This is the required uniform cubic constraint.

8. Use maximality

Let f satisfy the maximality condition in the statement. Thus for each n, f(n) is the greatest integer m such that every n-element finite set A satisfies

  m <= number of distinct prime divisors of P(A).

We claim that for every n,

  n<=16+8f(n)^3.                                                     (24)

Suppose instead that n>16+8f(n)^3. Let A be any n-element finite set, and let k be the number of distinct prime divisors of P(A). By (23),

  n<=16+8k^3.

If k<=f(n), then 16+8k^3<=16+8f(n)^3<n, a contradiction. Therefore k>=f(n)+1 for every n-element A. This says that f(n)+1 also has the defining uniform-lower-bound property. But f(n) was the greatest integer with that property, so it would follow that f(n)+1<=f(n), an impossibility. Hence (24) holds.

9. Passage to the limit

It remains to show that (24) implies

  f(n)/log n -> +infinity.

Let R be an arbitrary real number, and put C=max(R,1). The standard elementary asymptotic estimate

  (log n)^3/n -> 0

and also 16/n->0 show that

  16/n + 8C^3 (log n)^3/n -> 0.

Consequently, for all sufficiently large n (in particular, with n>1),

  16+8(C log n)^3<n.                                                 (25)

For such n, log n>0. If f(n)/log n<C, then f(n)<C log n, and therefore

  16+8f(n)^3 < 16+8(C log n)^3<n,

contradicting (24). Thus, eventually,

  f(n)/log n >= C >= R.

Because this holds for every real R, the sequence f(n)/log n tends to +infinity. This proves the conjectured statement.
